title: The Swiss Cheese Model of Building Failure

zones.label: Design Slice
zones.summary: The first defense: drawings and details that are meant to be both code-compliant and buildable.
facts: Chapter 21 lists design as a cause category; its Riverbend example is a window head drawn with no flashing detail.
A detail can meet the code and still be a hole, for example one that is too tight to install or that never says how two parts connect.
Design holes are often dormant: they sit on the drawings for months until the weather or a load finds them. Reason called such conditions latent.
A clear, buildable detail and a design review plug these holes before any product is ordered.

zones.label: Materials Slice
zones.summary: The second defense: the products delivered to the site must be the ones the designer assumed.
facts: Chapter 21's example is framing delivered wet, which starts a wall's life already carrying moisture.
A substituted product can look equivalent while differing in strength, fire rating, or how it handles moisture, so substitutions need review.
A hole here comes from the wrong product or one damaged in storage, and it passes unnoticed unless someone checks.
Tests that show whether products and systems perform are part of the inspection and testing checks in Chapter 17.

zones.label: Construction Slice
zones.summary: The third defense: the work must be built the way it was drawn, in the right order.
facts: Chapter 21 lists work not built as designed as a cause category; its example is flashing installed backward.
Many construction holes are small and later hidden: a missed lap, a skipped fastener, a gap that gets covered by the next trade.
Mockups, installer training, and the contractor's own checks plug these holes while the work is still visible.
Inspectors rely on this slice doing its job, because they see only a sample of the work (Chapter 17).

zones.label: Inspection Slice
zones.summary: The fourth defense: checks that are meant to catch what the earlier slices missed.
facts: The inspector sees only a sample of the work on a given day, and inspection does not replace the contractor's own quality control (Chapter 17).
Work that is covered before it is checked, such as flashing behind siding, cannot be inspected afterward without opening the wall.
A rushed or skipped inspection leaves a hole in the one slice whose job is to find holes in the others.
Inspection is also a slice that can be strengthened: special inspections and tests are covered in Chapter 17.

zones.label: Maintenance Slice
zones.summary: The last defense: upkeep that finds and fixes small problems for the whole life of the building.
facts: Chapter 21 calls neglect a leading reason that buildings fail early; its example is clogged roof drains.
A maintenance hole can stay open the longest, because it lasts for as long as the building does.
Preventive maintenance, scheduled servicing and inspection at set intervals, finds small problems before they become failures (Chapter 21).
An ignored leak or stain is the building telling you a hole in an earlier slice is already open.

zones.label: Failure Outcome
zones.summary: Where the arrow lands when the holes line up: mold, collapse, or fire spread, and in most cases something far milder.
facts: Chapter 21 describes building failure as a condition where a building no longer meets its required performance, from rare collapse to common leaks, cracks, and mold.
Failures are better understood by their causes than their symptoms; a stain on a ceiling can trace back to a drawing (Chapter 21).
The same pattern applies to fire: sprinklers, rated walls, alarms, and exits are layers whose holes seldom line up (Chapter 18).
Damage grows the longer the path stays open: in Chapter 21's example, rot takes hold within a few years.

zones.label: Three Generic Failure Chains
zones.summary: Three composite examples show the same pattern: a roof leak, a deck collapse, and a smoke-spread incident.
facts: Roof leak: a missed flashing in construction, a clogged drain in maintenance, and a skipped check in between let water reach the framing.
Deck collapse: a weak connection detail, the wrong fasteners substituted, and years of unseen rot let one load find an aligned path.
Smoke spread: an unsealed penetration through a rated wall and a propped door, with no one checking either, undo the compartment (Chapter 18).
These are composite teaching scenarios built from common failure types, not accounts of specific events.

zones.label: Redundancy and Offset Holes
zones.summary: The fix: independent defenses with holes that do not line up, so one mistake is caught by the next layer.
facts: Redundancy means more than one independent defense against the same hazard, such as a drainage gap behind the cladding plus flashing plus a water control layer.
Independence matters: two checks by the same person with the same assumption share a hole, so they do not add protection.
Chapter 21 says breaking a failure chain at any single link, in design, inspection, or early maintenance, would have prevented the loss.
Five slices is a teaching choice. A real project has other defenses too, such as testing, commissioning, and occupants reporting problems.

quiz.question: A window head is drawn with no flashing detail at all, and the crew builds exactly what the drawings show. Which slice holds the hole?
quiz.explanation: The omission is on the drawings, so the hole is in the first defense, before any work starts.

quiz.question: A truckload of framing lumber arrives soaked, and a cheaper sealant is swapped in without review. Which slice does this belong to?
quiz.explanation: Defective, damaged, or substituted products are holes in the defense that supplies the right components.

quiz.question: The drawings call for flashing lapped over the sheathing, but the crew installs it backward. Which slice is that hole in?
quiz.explanation: The work was not built as designed, which is a hole in the building stage.

quiz.question: An inspector visits for an hour and checks a sample of the work, and the flashing is already covered by siding. Which slice has a hole?
quiz.explanation: Inspection sees only a sample of the work, and covered work cannot be checked, so a hole can pass through.

quiz.question: Roof drains are clogged for years and a ceiling stain is ignored. Which slice is failing?
quiz.explanation: Skipped upkeep is the last defense failing, and it can stay open for the entire life of the building.

quiz.question: The arrow passes through all five aligned holes and reaches the building. What does this region show?
quiz.explanation: When holes in every defense line up, a hazard reaches the building and produces mold, collapse, or fire spread.

quiz.question: A teacher wants three composite scenarios to show that different failure types share the same pattern. Which region has them?
quiz.explanation: A roof leak, a deck collapse, and a smoke-spread incident each show several aligned holes, and none is a specific real event.

quiz.question: A project adds an independent drainage gap, flashing, and a second reviewer, so the holes no longer line up. Which region shows this fix?
quiz.explanation: Independent defenses with offset holes make it much less likely that a single mistake reaches the building.

quiz.question: Which slice is meant to catch the holes in the earlier ones but still has holes of its own, because it checks only a sample?
quiz.explanation: It is the defense whose job is to find other defenses' holes, and it relies on the earlier slices doing their own quality control.

quiz.question: A team lets one person both do the work and check it, using the same assumption. Which region explains why this adds little protection?
quiz.explanation: Two checks that share the same assumption share the same hole, so independence matters more than the number of checks.
